item.title: Victoria’s Secret Brings Back the Fantasy Bra — and an Old Stereotype of Sexy
item.description:
The big reveal of the 2026 Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show came about three-quarters of the way through the extravaganza.

It came after Bella Hadid had strutted out in stilettos, a bejeweled bra with matching panties and wings made to resemble a pointillist garden, like some sort of Seurat-inspired boudoir mirage. After Megan Moroney, in baby pink marabou wings, had serenaded a section featuring supermodels as sexy flower fairies and Tate McRae had writhed around in a crimson corset and matching stockings amid a sea of similarly writhing women in crimson lingerie.

It came after the “Pink” section, with Katseye as naughty schoolgirls and Trinity Rodman in sequined hot pants and a push-up bra. (Also, oddly, a lot of puppy dog handbags and puppy dog charms, because, apparently, we are no longer stereotyping young women as sex kittens and are now stereotyping them as … sex puppies? Progress!)

And the unveiling came with a lot of dramatic backlighting to build anticipation. Then, finally: ta-da!

The Fantasy Bra: a $50 million creation by Jacob Arabo of Jacob & Co. featuring a 75.54-carat vivid yellow diamond amid 4,410 white diamonds, modeled by Kylie Jenner, with her own set of unicorn-like wings and a wisp of a sheer miniskirt, for modesty. Or at least the suggestion of it.

It was the first time a fantasy bra, once the centerpiece of the show, had been seen on a Victoria’s Secret runway since 2018.

As such, it was the final variable in a return to form for Victoria’s Secret that has been taking shape over the past two years. First, the brand brought back the runway, which was canceled in 2019 as ties between Les Wexner, then the company’s owner, and Jeffrey Epstein, were exposed, and then revived in 2024). Then it brought back the Angels, who were retired in 2021 in favor of a woman-focused collective, then unretired two years ago. It even brought back Gisele Bündchen, the most famous Angel of all, who made a cameo video languorously reclining on her sofa in little lacy nothings before this year’s show. (There were rumors that she was going to walk the runway, but a broken foot just beforehand seemed to put an end to that.) And it brought the show back to Los Angeles for the first time in nearly 20 years.

But in bringing back the Fantasy Bra, the brand’s leaders weren’t just revealing an extravagant new piece of intimate couture. They were revealing just how much we have reverted to pre-#MeToo definitions of sexy and how little change has actually occurred, despite all of the soul-searching and existential crises of the early 2020s about how a brand that put women on display like dream dolls of the bedroom may have contributed to a culture of sexual harassment and abuse. Amid all of the hooting and catcalling for Jenner, including by her boyfriend, Timothée Chalamet, and her mother, Kris Jenner, both sitting in the front row, that disappearing idea may have been the most transparent look of all.

It’s almost as if the past seven years didn’t happen.

After all, VS may position the show as an expression of self-confidence and joy. The chief executive, Hillary Super, and Adam Selman, the creative director, may talk about giving women ownership of their own bodies, and there may be a variety of those bodies on display, with Nicole Kidman cheering on from the front row. But there’s no getting away from the reality that the VS show is perpetrating a very specific Vargas girl-Playboy tradition of sexy.

One that is all about the legs! And the boobs! And the bottom! It’s cloaking the promise of transgression in the trappings of the cherub, then putting it on display for everyone to see.

According to Selman, this is all in the service of what the VS customer wants. VS decided to bring back the Fantasy Bra because fans were asking for it, he said. He christened this year’s show, which also included a performance by Megan Thee Stallion, “Fandemonium.” And it’s clearly working: The company’s share price has surged this year.

So maybe the whole bustier-’n-knickers babe look is most women’s dream, as it clearly was most men’s. By reverting to these old gender stereotypes, VS is reverting to a time when “sexy” was defined by the male gaze and catering to it. The company may have changed its stock market ticker listing to VSXY from VSCO in June to reflect its new mission, but there is nothing particularly new about this idea.

Or maybe what this is about is a nostalgia for a time when we could pretend that this way of presenting women was just lighthearted fun and didn’t contribute directly to a culture that enabled their objectification and depersonalization — even though we know that such a time is as much a fantasy as the fantasy bra. Watching the VS show after the national conversation prompted by the crisis at Cornell is a bit like entering the twilight zone. Though it does go with another national conversation, one in which men are men and women are women and you can tell by how they dress.

But here’s the thing: Victoria’s Secret may make undergarments, but they are still garments. It is still a fashion brand. And fashion is at its best when it gives people the thing they didn’t know they wanted: the thing that offers them a new, powerful way to be themselves in the world.

Wouldn’t it be incredible if, rather than simply reviving the past and resorting to sexy clichés, Selman and co. managed to think of a new way to communicate physical agency and unfetter the body? If what everyone saw on the VS runway wasn’t what they were expecting but a whole new idea about lingerie entirely?

Maybe that’s the real fantasy. If they could pull it off, this particular fashion form might actually take wing.

item.title: How Do Airports Prepare for Disaster? With Fake Screams and Cloth Dummies.
item.description:
An urgent message rang through the nerve center of Kennedy International Airport in New York City at 10 a.m. on Saturday. An aircraft, it said, had crashed at the airport.

Details were scant: “Unknown souls on board, unknown fuel on board,” the announcement said.

The simulated emergency had begun.

As the first fire trucks hurried to the scene, representatives from local, state and federal agencies gathered in the Emergency Operations Center, inside a nondescript airport office building, where they would spend the next couple of hours managing the mock crisis. Radio chatter filled the room. Officials fielded phone calls and watched the response on a giant screen.

The Federal Aviation Administration mandates that commercial airports hold a full-scale emergency exercise every three years to test responding agencies’ ability to coordinate swiftly and safely.

The New York Times was granted exclusive access to this simulation, which lasted about two hours and involved more than 100 emergency responders from agencies including the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, the New York Police Department, the New York Fire Department, Customs and Border Protection, the Transportation Security Administration and the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

This was the first full-scale drill at a major New York City-area airport since the deadly collision between an Air Canada jet and an airport fire truck at LaGuardia Airport in March. (Other types of emergency exercises are held more frequently and have taken place since then.)

Sarah McKeon, the director of aviation for the Port Authority, which runs Kennedy, LaGuardia and Newark Liberty International Airport, credited frequent training exercises for what she called an effective response to the LaGuardia accident, in which all 72 passengers survived but the two pilots died.

In a real emergency, “one of the biggest challenges is a safe and orderly response,” she said in an interview during the simulation. “That real-world test of our emergency plans was a testament to the fact that we do so much preparedness and testing,” she added.

A convoy of emergency vehicles descended upon the scene of the staged crash, tucked in a corner of the airfield away from the runways and out of view of the terminals. Dozens of firefighters and paramedics raced to evacuate passengers down staircases from the jet’s rear doors and move everyone to safety.

Details began to emerge: The aircraft was an international arrival with 102 people on board.

Victims howled and screamed for help, some of them carried away by firefighters and others triaged on the tarmac. Officials set up a mobile command center and a reunification point nearby. Smoke wafted over the alarming scene.

The victims were pretending; the smoke came from a machine. The jet, an undamaged Airbus A330-900 belonging to Delta Air Lines, did not have its escape slides deployed, and unlike a real crash scene, this one had no debris field from an aircraft.

Still, “the drill itself is very realistic,” said Jason Jankowski, the deputy chief of aircraft rescue and firefighting, known as ARFF, at Kennedy. Mr. Jankowski was a battalion chief at LaGuardia when the Air Canada crash happened. That accident, partly attributed to a fire truck operating without a transponder, led the Port Authority to move to install trackers on its emergency vehicles.

During the drill, Fire Department and ARFF units worked together to extinguish an imaginary blaze. Mr. Jankowski called that collaboration essential. “I don’t get to work side by side with the F.D.N.Y. very often, and I don’t want the first time that I work side by side with them to be at an actual emergency,” he said.

A Snozzle, an extendable arm designed to pierce the fuselage of an aircraft to deliver water or firefighting foam inside, stood at the ready, mounted on a truck.

“In a real accident, this whole area would be covered in foam,” Ms. McKeon said, gesturing to the area around the jet.

Emergency responders did not receive details of the scenario ahead of time. The Port Authority said in a written statement that the element of surprise was “essential for effectively testing the airport’s emergency plan.” Past drills have simulated a water rescue and an aircraft that crashed into a terminal.

More than 100 volunteers, many of them students or members of local service groups, played the victims. All wore white T-shirts and tags around their necks describing their injuries. Some were taken on gurneys to a line of ambulances waiting nearby. Others sprawled on the ground, shouting “Help me!” Police officers escorted those who could walk away from the scene, where they waited in buses or checked in with officials at the reunification point.

Luggage was scattered around the aircraft. Among the bags, a few fabric dummies, also with tags, represented the deceased. Emergency responders later moved the dummies to a side area for examination.

Set back from the aircraft, officials packed into the incident command center, a bus-like communications hub, to coordinate between the accident site and the Emergency Operations Center.

Teresa Rizzuto, the general manager of Kennedy Airport, explained that officials in the command center kept track of where each responding unit was deployed, directing resources to the site as needed. Mr. Jankowski tracked his fire trucks on a hand-held white board.

Outside the command center, two passengers who escaped without serious injuries described to a Port Authority police officer what they experienced in the moments leading up to the simulated crash.

Now, a crowd of passengers was growing at the reunification point.

Survivors shouted questions, some in Spanish and Portuguese, at airline and airport staff. One asked whether she could still get a connecting flight to Miami without her belongings. Another wondered whether he would be deported because he had lost his passport during the evacuation. An airport representative offered them vague reassurances and told the crowd that they would be housed and fed, connected with family and reunited with their baggage if possible.

After the simulation, agency leaders gathered to discuss what went well and what needed improvement.

To ensure officials could speak frankly about their takeaways, The Times was not permitted to attend the review. But in a video interview on Monday, Ms. Rizzuto said the drill had achieved its objectives.

“The exercise totally reinforced the confidence, and the ability, of our airport and our emergency response partners to work together efficiently in a real emergency,” she said.

One area that could have benefited from more preparation, she said, was communication at the reunification point, which was added on the tarmac for the first time in this drill following recommendations that emerged after the midair collision of an American Airlines jet and an Army Black Hawk helicopter near Washington in 2025.

But the exercise, she said, clearly demonstrated the strength of the airport’s emergency plans: “This just adds to the confidence level that we will be ready, God forbid.”

Follow New York Times Travel on Instagram and sign up for our Travel Dispatch newsletter to get expert tips on traveling smarter and inspiration for your next vacation. Dreaming up a future getaway or just armchair traveling? Check out our 52 Places to Go in 2026.

item.title: See a Knicks Opener for Under $1,000? Oh, Those Were the Pre-Title Days.
item.description:
This summer, Ankit Kakkad, a New York Knicks season-ticket holder, thought it was a great idea to sell his ticket to Game 4 of the N.B.A. finals for about $28,000. The money would cover his Knicks season tickets for about the next two and a half seasons.

He felt even better about the decision when the team went down by 29 points. But as the Knicks clawed back in the second half, regret crept in. It escalated as the team pulled off one of the greatest comebacks in league history, with a last-second tip-in by OG Anunoby.

“If I’m being rational, absolutely it was the right move to make,” he said recently.

But Mr. Kakkad, 42, is not rational. He is a Knicks fan. He had believed every year of his life that the Knicks would win a championship. He believes last year’s Knicks team was perhaps the greatest team in N.B.A. history.

This kind of enthusiasm is part of what drives the sports ticket market.

Knicks tickets have never been cheap, but their championship last season means that now a single ticket can cost more than a vacation in Paris, or a month’s rent in a midsize American city. The team’s home, Madison Square Garden, is the most expensive place to watch a game in the N.B.A. Prices for tickets this season, which starts on Tuesday, are averaging nearly twice what they did last season on the secondary market, including on sites like StubHub and SeatGeek.

The average price for the Knicks season opener on Tuesday is $1,894, according to the ticket reselling site TickPick, the highest average price ever for a regular-season N.B.A. game. Many tickets were going for more than $5,000.

“My impression is that people are resigned to the fact that it’s New York City and it’s the Knicks, and the Knicks are winning and the ticket prices are just going to be high,” said Jonathan Macri, who hosts a podcast called “Knicks Film School.” He said he had never seen as much demand for Knicks tickets as during the past few years, during the team’s ascent.

The Knicks’ season opener isn’t a typical regular-season game. The players will receive their championship rings and hang a banner for the team’s first championship in 53 years. They will play the Philadelphia 76ers, where LeBron James signed this summer. That’s partly why, as of Monday morning, the cheapest ticket available for the game was $1,000 — $786 more than the cheapest ticket for last year’s Knicks season opener.

And while the Knicks don’t control the secondary market, the prices they do control are rising, too. The Knicks have a policy not to raise ticket prices after missing the playoffs, but they have made the playoffs the past four seasons.

A few weeks ago, when the Knicks released single-game tickets for their season opener, the cheapest was more than $1,000. The Knicks responded to fans’ outrage by saying those prices were a mistake. The team gave refunds of hundreds or sometimes thousands of dollars to those who had paid the initial high prices. In a statement, the Knicks said ticket prices would revert to last season’s prices plus an increase of 12 percent.

Season-ticket prices have been increasing about that much, too.

Dashiell Desloovere, a longtime fan, has the least expensive quarter-season plan, in the arena’s 200 level. For 11 games, his seat went from $1,276 last season to $1,430 this season.

“My wife says the Knicks were my first love,” said Mr. Desloovere, who couldn’t afford Knicks tickets when he was growing up on the Upper East Side. “So she’s OK with me being crazy when I watch them.”

The Action Network, a sports media company that focuses on sports betting, conducted a study that found Madison Square Garden to be the priciest N.B.A. arena this season. The study analyzed more than 300,000 tickets from each of the league’s 30 teams and estimated that a family of four could pay $1,930.55 to buy four tickets, two beers, two soft drinks, four hot dogs and one parking space to see the Knicks. The N.B.A. average was $954.64.

Overall, the study found that prices across the league had risen an average of 12.8 percent. Knicks ticket prices increased 27.2 percent, which was the seventh-highest increase in the league.

“It’s amazing how they don’t consider the average man,” said John Gravagna, who grew up in Flushing, Queens, and had season tickets from 1998 until about 10 years ago when he found it difficult to sell or even give away his tickets. Sports, he argued, are different from other forms of entertainment because “it creeps into the fabric of your family.”

The timing of this kind of pricing bump isn’t a new phenomenon.

In 2005, the Holy Cross economics professors Victor Matheson and Robert Baade wrote that from 1983 and 2000, the average National Football League team had raised ticket prices 6 percent each year, but Super Bowl-winning teams increased them 12 percent. That section of the paper is titled, “Championships, the gift that keeps on taking.”

What’s new, Mr. Matheson said, is that the demand for premium experiences has risen sharply since the Covid-19 pandemic.

“High diesel prices and high beef prices aren’t affecting the folks who own a $5.5 million townhouse in Manhattan,” he said. “Those folks have been doing quite well.” He added: “Those are the folks that are buying the finals tickets. Not the schoolteacher, not the police officer, not the restaurant worker.”

For Mr. Kakkad, the regret of selling the ticket to Game 4 wore off quickly. He still watched at a bar with his friends, and celebrated with Knicks fans.

The entire playoff run took on a special meaning for him. His mother died in April, early in the Knicks’ championship run, and he turned to the team to distract him from his pain. They won and won and won.

“That was my mom looking out for me, right? Making sure she gave me something to look forward to,” he said recently. “This run probably saved me in a lot of ways.”

This year, Mr. Kakkad’s season tickets went from about $10,000 per seat for the season to a little more than $11,000. He works in I.T. and said Knicks season tickets were a splurge he allowed himself, noting he doesn’t have many expenses and doesn’t have children. But the situation with ticket prices does unsettle him.

“Fans are of all backgrounds,” he said. “New York Knicks fans, true fans, are absolutely priced out. I mean think about any of the playoff games, like what average fan can afford that? I’m never dropping 20 grand on a ticket.”

item.title: Trump Announces $8 Billion Plan to Cover Farm Losses
item.description:
President Trump said at a rally in Kansas Monday night that the Agriculture Department would provide $8 billion in economic aid to farmers hurt by high diesel prices.

It was the second time in two years that the president authorized billions of dollars in bailout money for farmers harmed by his administration’s policies, and came 15 days before a midterm election in which unhappy farmers and ranchers could be the deciding votes in close races across the country.

Under the plan, known as the Harvest Fuel Relief Program, the Agriculture Department will use a formula based on how many acres and which crops farmers planted to reimburse them for a “portion” of their losses. The money will come from the Commodity Credit Corporation, a financing institution that the Agriculture Department uses to fund crop insurance and natural disaster payment programs.

Payment rates will be announced next month, and farmers will receive money at a later date.

Farmers use diesel in their machinery and irrigation systems, especially in the fall when they run combine harvesters. The price of a gallon of diesel has averaged $6 or more in most of the country in recent weeks, compared with about $3.50 last fall, saddling many farmers with thousands of dollars in additional costs.

Higher diesel prices have hit farmers unevenly. According to the Farm Bureau, a lobby group, the production cost to grow an acre of wheat rose by $6 because of higher fuel costs, while the cost to grow an acre of rice rose by $52. Fertilizer costs, which are closely tied to fuel costs, also went up this spring and summer.

Farmers are traditionally a solid Republican voting bloc. But high fuel and fertilizer costs, along with tariffs and trade disruptions, are dragging down the electoral prospects of a number of Republican candidates in what were thought to be solidly Republican areas.

Mr. Trump was rallying for Senator Roger Marshall, a Kansas Republican, outside of Wichita on Monday night. Mr. Marshall comfortably won election in 2020 by 11 points, but most polls show the he is tied or running slightly behind his Democratic challenger, Adam Hamilton. National Republican groups have been diverting money to Kansas to shore up Mr. Marshall’s chances.

In announcing the aid for farmers, Mr. Trump sought to credit it to Mr. Marshall. “Roger Marshall is the leader who fought for that to happen,” he said.

Neither the president nor the Agriculture Department explained the causes of higher diesel prices:

During the early months of the war in Iran, oil exports through the Persian Gulf nearly ground to a halt, driving up prices. The flow of oil and refined fuel has resumed — with the help of the U.S. military — but volumes are still below prewar levels.

The rescue package came two weeks after the president announced a more modest executive order to help farmers with high diesel prices at a rally in a different Midwest farm state, Nebraska.

That order allowed the use so-called dyed diesel — which typically can only be used in off-road machinery like tractors — in on-road vehicles, and defers and possibly eliminates some taxes on it. The amount of money that farmers were estimated to save from the dyed diesel order was far less than the $8 billion they were set to receive through the Harvest Fuel Relief Program.

The latest rescue package mirrored the $12 billion Farmer Bridge Assistance Program the Agriculture Department rolled out in December. That was called an “economic loss program” and came after months of lower-than-usual exports of American crops because of the Trump administration’s tariff and trade policies.

item.title: Investors Await Musk’s Next Big SpaceX Deal
item.description:
Andrew here. How high can energy prices go without hurting the stock market? Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil, topped $110 a barrel this morning, yet surprisingly — unless you believe that strong corporate earnings mean energy costs don’t matter — the stock market has stayed calm.

But if oil stays here or climbs higher, companies’ bottom lines could get squeezed. We’re focusing on earnings this week, as heavyweights like Netflix, G.M. and United Airlines report, as well as SpaceX, which we get into below.

When SpaceX reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday, there will be plenty of things for Wall Street to keep an eye on.

Investors and analysts will study Elon Musk’s trillion-dollar colossus over its artificial intelligence spending. And then there’s the question of whether Musk will announce a long-awaited combination of SpaceX with Tesla (which reports earnings on Wednesday).

SpaceX is increasingly an A.I. story. Tech stocks went up on Monday, as investors appeared to set aside their worries about the scale and speed of the A.I. buildout. Companies like Anthropic have continued to demonstrate a hunger for computing power — a need that SpaceX is betting on by building huge, and hugely expensive, data centers.

Last quarter, SpaceX’s A.I. spending exploded to $15.8 billion in the quarter, more than double its previous quarterly outlay.

Wall Street watchers are less concerned about whether SpaceX can get the financing than about how much doing so will cost, Adam Jonas, an analyst at Morgan Stanley, wrote in a recent research note.

Also watch Starlink, the satellite internet service that generates a majority of SpaceX’s revenue. Analysts will look to see whether the business is still growing strongly, after revenue rose 66 percent year on year last quarter.

SpaceX recently battered U.S. telecom stocks with its deal to buy billions of dollars’ worth of wireless spectrum, raising the prospect of it offering cellular phone service. But it also faces challenges in Europe: Several telecom companies there announced plans to explore creating a satellite mobile phone service.

Pay attention to what Musk says about Ukraine, after Volodymyr Zelensky, the country’s president, complained about his forces’ access to the military version of Starlink. Musk recently declared that it’s “time for Zelensky to go.”

What about a Tesla tie-up? Investors have long speculated that Musk would seek to unite the two companies, as he has done again and again.

Some on Wall Street have speculated whether that transaction could be announced before year end. But uniting the two makes sense, Gene Munster, whose Deepwater Asset Management is invested in both companies, told DealBook’s Brian O’Keefe:

If Elon’s master plan is around A.I., which he’s been talking about forever, then in order to have a true A.I. company, you have to have the physical side, the terrestrial side. It’s like three quarters or half a vision without Tesla.

Saudi Arabia postpones its big investment conference. The Future Investment Initiative Institute said that its annual meeting, which was set to take place next week and feature speakers like Jamie Dimon of JPMorgan Chase and Larry Fink of BlackRock, would take place next year. The long-awaited move came amid concerns about security, as the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen attack Saudi targets like an international airport in the kingdom.

The engineer accused of bugging OpenAI stays in jail. A federal judge ordered the now-former employee, Abdulrahman Alfozan, to remain in custody without bail. Prosecutors accused Alfozan, whom the company accused of planting a recording device in an office, of having extensive ties to the Saudi government; a Saudi Consulate offered to cover Alfozan’s bail, according to his lawyers.

President Trump says he’s open to meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping. Trump told reporters on Monday that he would consider meeting his Russian and Chinese counterparts — but about denuclearization, even as Putin suggested that such a gathering would focus on ending the war in Ukraine. Trump’s apparent siding with Putin against Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukraine’s president, has drawn criticism even from Republicans.

Calm returned to Paris and other French cities overnight. But investors remain spooked by protests over the weekend that devolved into riots.

Parisians crunched through shards of glasses and burned debris on Tuesday, tallying losses from looted stores and bracing for more demonstrations. Government curfews imposed last night in several neighborhoods emptied cafes usually filled with tourists and locals, deepening a sense of unrest that threatens to spread throughout Europe, Vivienne Walt reports from Paris.

The latest:

The CAC 40, France’s benchmark stock index, fell, as did other European indexes.

Rioters targeted retailers, including the luxury brands Louis Vuitton and Hermès. Insurers are expecting at least a €1 billion hit from the violence over the weekend, according to Morningstar DBRS.

The yield on France’s 10-year government bond rebounded. But Monday’s sell-off pushed the gap between French and German government bond yields — an indicator of Europe’s stability — to a level last seen in 2012.

European economies have been hit hard. A cost-of-living crisis and a debt crunch have driven up yields across much of the world since the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran sent oil prices skyrocketing.

That, along with Europe’s slow-growth outlook, puts the European Central Bank in a bind.

France seems especially vulnerable. One analyst told Le Point that there was a “high” probability that the country’s credit rating would be downgraded as soon as this week.

European contagion? There are concerns that the protests — stemming from rising costs and other grievances — could spread to other countries. Demonstrations have occurred in Milan, Brussels and elsewhere in recent days.

Social media accounts associated with the “yellow vest” protest movement in France announced demonstrations for Saturday to express broad anger about rising inflation and stagnant pay.

Emmanuel Macron appears out of options. Unlike in previous political crises, Macron, the French president, has little money to throw at the problem, analysts say. France’s debt burden has hit 119 percent of G.D.P., and parliamentarians have feuded for weeks over how to carry out €54 billion ($60.5 billion) in cuts.

Macron, a former investment banker, actively courted international businesses to invest in France. He cannot run in the April presidential election because of term limits — and the turmoil could hand Marine Le Pen, the far-right leader whose France-first economic policies have alarmed some economists, a decisive boost in that race.

The S.E.C. recently shook up the world of stock trading, issuing an order to help usher in trading of tokenized shares in the U.S.

This month, OKXICE became the first tokenized stock trading venue. It was born out of a joint venture between the crypto exchange ​OKX and Intercontinental Exchange, the owner of the N.Y.S.E.

The platform is already facing backlash from companies that don’t want their shares tokenized, Niko Gallogly reports.

The context: A tokenized stock is a digital token recorded on a blockchain whose trading price tracks the shares of a publicly listed company.

Proponents, including crypto enthusiasts and some traditional finance firms, say it is a more efficient way to trade and track share ownership.

But OKXICE has drawn pushback from corporate issuers, traditional exchanges and market makers. They argue that it bypasses traditional investor protections including:

Best-execution pricing, which requires trading prices to reflect the real-time value of a stock. With tokenized stock platforms like OKXICE, prices are set according to the ratio of tokens in the platform’s trading pool, not by the broader market for the underlying stock. That could cause deviation between the two prices.

The liability and compliance protection provided to issuing companies by the S.E.C.’s market surveillance, which helps detect insider trading and other forms of market manipulation. Instead, OKXICE said it relied on internal surveillance and other third parties to provide those safeguards.

An S.E.C. spokesperson declined to comment. Intercontinental Exchange did not respond to a request for comment. OKX pointed DealBook to comments in The Wall Street Journal by Andrew Cuomo, the former governor of New York, that called the exchange the future of stock trading and more. Cuomo is a chair of the joint venture.

For now, it’s ruffling feathers. “If you’ve just done a huge I.P.O., paid Goldman Sachs to run and price your offering, then suddenly someone sets up another venue where your stock can be traded 24/7 outside of your control and at prices that may vary from traditional markets,” Gareth Rhodes, a former deputy superintendent at the New York State Department of Financial Services, told DealBook, “you might be like ‘Yeah, we don’t want that.’”

Another issue: Tokenized stock-trading platforms typically don’t need approval from companies to tokenize stocks.

Instead, companies have a 30-day window to opt out — and many have. Verizon, Broadcom, CoreWeave and UnitedHealth have objected to having their shares traded by OKXICE.

Artificial intelligence is increasingly moving out of the digital world and into the physical one, including manufacturing.

Arda Industries, a start-up that aims to integrate the technology into factories, is emerging from stealth mode and announcing a $232 million Series A fund-raising round at a $1.5 billion valuation, Sri Muppidi is first to report.

What Arda does: The company helps manufacturing engineers do their work in one software platform instead of using multiple tools, and keep work updated as designs change.

Arda’s C.E.O., Bob McGrew, described the company as building an “I.D.E. for manufacturing engineering,” referring to an integrated development environment used to write, run and test code in one place.

The company also plans to use A.I. agents for robots, something it hopes will cut the time needed to reconfigure assembly lines to days from months.

Arda generates revenue based on the number of tasks that its agentic tools perform, McGrew said.

It was founded by A.I. veterans: McGrew was most recently the chief research officer at OpenAI. He previously worked at Palantir alongside two of Arda’s other founders, Alex Mark and Jakob Frick. The other Arda founder, Augustus Odena, helped create the A.I. start-up Adept, which Amazon “acqui-hired.”

The investors in the round: Altimeter Capital, Accel and Khosla Ventures led the round. Other participants included Felicis, XYZ Venture Capital and 8VC.

Arda’s backers argue that it could make U.S. manufacturing more competitive:

The vision is for companies to “build something quickly to their specification onshore and know the whole lineage of the supply chain,” Steve Loughlin, a partner at Accel, told DealBook.

Peter Deng, a general partner at Felicis and a former colleague of McGrew’s at OpenAI, said tools like Arda’s could help the U.S. build “the first truly A.I.-native industrial base.”

Arda is working with military and data center companies, McGrew told DealBook. One is Anduril, the A.I. defense start-up whose founders include Palmer Luckey, which is reportedly in talks to let insiders sell shares at a roughly $90 billion valuation.

Deals

The activist investor Starboard has reportedly built up a stake in Solstice Advanced Materials, seeking changes in the company’s strategy to bolster its stock price. (FT)

The law firm Freshfields apologized “unreservedly” for comments senior leaders made about “probably” excluding Middle Eastern investors from any deal involving its artificial intelligence division. (FT)

item.title: A ‘Doom Loop’ Threatens France as Populism Confronts Markets
item.description:
When protests over high gas prices ripped through France in 2018, President Emmanuel Macron offered to enact about $11 billion in tax cuts and wage increases to try to quell the unrest.

Today, after protests over education turned violent, Mr. Macron is in no position to use money to bring calm to the streets.

That’s because the French government is also fighting the prospect of a crisis in its bond market. Investors have been dumping French debt, unsure of the government’s ability to manage its budget amid high interest rates and political uncertainty.

Announcing a big financial commitment to mollify protesters would likely rattle investors further and lead to another jump in the government’s borrowing costs. Mr. Macron, approaching the end of his time in office, is leading a centrist government without a governing majority. He is left in a tight spot: Both inaction and more spending could exacerbate France’s troubles and give populist politicians running for his seat next year a bigger opening to attract aggravated voters.

France is not the only country facing a debt trap. As borrowing grows in many wealthy nations, populist political parties are surging. Experts warn the mix could combust into an economic crisis.

Governments face a “doom loop,” in which market turmoil and political tumult feed off each other, according to Michal Brzozowski and Joanna Siwinska-Gorzelak, researchers at Poland’s University of Warsaw, who published a research paper on the relationship between populism and fiscal policy.

“The risk is less about a sudden debt default and more about a slow-motion economic drag,” they wrote in an email.

At the root of the problem is a considerable tension: Amid deep political and fiscal uncertainty, voters and investors appear to want different things.

Buyers of debt want to be adequately compensated for the risk of lending to governments. In turn they are shunning lawmakers who seem unable to make difficult choices, such as spending cuts or tax increases, to reduce yawning budget deficits. They are demanding higher interest payments, amid expectations that governments will keep borrowing a lot. This dynamic is unfolding most forcefully in France, but Germany, Japan and the United States are also contending with higher borrowing costs.

Voters, though, are increasingly turning to populist parties that largely reject the idea that budgets require painful trade-offs. Instead, they promise to protect generous retirement programs and other spending, while often proposing to cut taxes.

The resulting tension could spiral like this: Economically anxious voters turn to extreme populists, who promise a pain-free return to better days, and buyers of government debt recoil.

In France, the government bond yields, a measure of borrowing costs, have climbed to the highest since 2002. And in another worrisome sign, the gap between yields on French and German 10-year government debt has jumped to its widest since 2011. German yields are typically lower than French ones, but the growing difference shows that investors are demanding an ever higher premium to hold French debt.

Source: Investing.com.

By The New York Times

Not all of the turmoil in bond markets comes from government policies. One of the largest triggers for rising bond yields worldwide has been the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. Higher energy prices have revived inflation and forced several central banks to raise interest rates.

No matter the cause, higher yields aggravate the already difficult situation facing some governments, which must spend more on debt interest payments at the expense of other priorities like education.

In Europe, where economic growth is lackluster, fiscal policy must do much of the hard work of reducing debt burdens. But raising taxes or cutting spending has been frequently met with strong public resistance because people already feel overtaxed and demand more in public services and welfare benefits.

Eventually these problems will come to a head, said Simon Radford, the director for policy and programming for the Milken Institute in Europe.

“If you’re not going to solve it with new growth, and if interest payments are outrunning growth, then eventually what can’t go on forever, won’t go on forever,” he said.

The turmoil in France began as demonstrations by high school students who wanted better classrooms and more teachers. Protests over the cost of living and funding for education and other services have spread through Europe, including in Belgium and Italy.

These financial troubles are particularly a problem for centrist political parties, said Ludovic Subran, the chief investment officer and chief economist at Allianz, the German insurance company. In many cases, these politicians want to use pledges of fiscal discipline to attract voters. But it often doesn’t work and instead and can leave the public with the impression that those politicians are largely powerless to improve conditions, he added.

“That’s really the Catch-22 of politics today,” Mr. Subran said. The politicians who have felt the disciplinary hand of the market are punished politically. “Then it gives extreme parties a boulevard to say whatever they want to say,” he added.

In Germany, the far-right Alternative for Germany party, or AfD, won a pair of state elections last month and now leads national polls. Its leaders have criticized the incumbent government, led by the center-right Chancellor Friedrich Merz, for proposals meant to shore up future budgets — including changes in some pension plans and a gradual raising of the retirement age.

In Britain, the center-left Labour government has been trying to fend off the rise of Reform U.K., a far-right party led by Nigel Farage. Earlier this year, as Reform led in the polls, the Labour Party ousted Keir Starmer as prime minister, who prioritized keeping bond markets calm, in favor of Andy Burnham, a mayor from a city in Northern England who promised sweeping changes to how the country was run.

France is at the sharp end of this predicament in Europe.

Even in 2018, Mr. Macron’s plan to stop the protests caused tremors in the bond market. The government promised its extra spending would be paid for by budget cuts and the deficit would stay in line with European limits. Today, the fiscal situation is much tougher. The annual budget deficit and the public debt, which is nearly 120 percent of the size of the French economy, are much larger than they were in 2018.

While holding emergency meetings about the protests, France’s prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, is trying to pass a budget for next year to narrow the deficit. But his minority government is facing stiff opposition as parties prepare for a presidential election in about six months. The far-right leader Marine Le Pen is the current front-runner, and polls suggest that she would face off against a far-left candidate.

Though Ms. Le Pen has proposed a vow to reduce the deficit, economists question the credibility of her financial plan, which would lower the retirement age while slashing spending on state bodies and cutting the country’s contribution to the European Union. All those measures would be difficult to enact. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the far-left candidate, has alarmed investors by proposing to effectively cancel some of the country’s debt instead of repaying it.

France faces “triple uncertainty” because of budget negotiations, the presidential election and legislative elections that are likely to follow soon after, said Mr. Subran, the Allianz economist. Therefore, France’s bond yields might not come down soon.

“A lot of people are holding their breath,” he said.

The cost of high yields will be felt quickly. The French government expects to spend more than 90 billion euros ($100 billion) on debt interest payments next year, which is more than planned spending on defense and education, according to the French finance ministry, another political headache.

item.title: Trump Tariffs on Canada Spark Latest Lawsuit Over Trade Powers
item.description:
A legal group that has successfully sued to scuttle President Trump’s past tariffs filed another court challenge on Tuesday, this time targeting the steep duties that he has imposed as part of an ongoing trade war with Canada.

The lawsuit marked the fourth major case brought by the Liberty Justice Center, which once again asked a panel of federal judges to invalidate Mr. Trump’s actions on grounds that he had overstepped the law in ways that harmed American businesses.

The emerging battle concerned the president’s use of Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, a long-dormant section of a decades-old trade statute meant to protect U.S. industry from unreasonable foreign practices. In September, Mr. Trump became the first president to enforce that power as part of a trade spat with Canada, which he has accused of discriminating against American industries.

The president’s tariffs, set at 50 percent, applied to a small yet shifting set of Canadian imports, including some alcoholic beverages, dairy products, hockey sticks, paper goods and more. Mr. Trump chose those items based on a belief that Ottawa had applied undue burdens to certain categories of U.S. products, a move that quickly prompted Canada to retaliate — and set off a tit-for-tat cycle that threatened to damage both economies.

The Liberty Justice Center filed its lawsuit on behalf of Gellert Global Group, a food importer and distributor based in New Jersey, which said it could face an estimated $40 million annually in taxes applied to Canadian cheese. The case challenged both Mr. Trump’s specific implementation of the duties and the broader constitutionality of Section 338.

The fate of Mr. Trump’s tactics now rests with the Court of International Trade, a specialized circuit that has repeatedly ruled against the White House and its tariffs in recent months. A victory could further embolden Mr. Trump against Canada or other countries, while a defeat would force the administration to pay back the money it has collected.

“The Section 338 tariffs are the administration’s latest attempt to exercise, through a statute never designed for the purpose, the tariff power that the Constitution assigns to Congress,” the lawsuit argued.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The lawsuit over Section 338 marked the latest legal headache for Mr. Trump and his economic agenda, which relies on sweeping tariffs to boost domestic manufacturing and raise new revenue. To date, the president’s multiple losses in court have backfired in one key respect, forcing the administration to pay back billions of dollars, plus interest, in illegally collected duties.

The string of defeats began with Mr. Trump’s use of an economic emergency law at the start of his second term to impose stiff duties on nearly every U.S. trading partner. The move drew a challenge by the Liberty Justice Center along with other businesses and state officials, which together prevailed at the Supreme Court in February.

Mr. Trump then imposed a 10 percent duty globally as a temporary replacement, only to draw successful lawsuits from some of the same opponents. They also targeted Mr. Trump’s third set of duties applied this year to dozens of countries, all accused of unfair trade practices. That case reached the Court of International Trade in late September.

The fight centered on Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which has been used by presidents of both parties to impose tariffs in response to unfair foreign trade practices. While the law itself is uncontroversial, a panel of judges seemed skeptical during oral arguments about Mr. Trump’s specific use of it, though the court has not yet ruled on the matter.

A precursor to that law is Section 338, which permits tariffs on countries that place “unequal impositions or discriminations” on American goods but not on the rest of the world. In a series of proclamations dating back to the summer, Mr. Trump accused Canada of such practices, then later invoked a lesser-known provision of that same law to ban some Canadian imports entirely.

In its new lawsuit, the Liberty Justice Center claimed that Mr. Trump’s proclamations did not follow the letter of the law, citing a series of what it called procedural mishaps with the timing and rollout of the duties. It said that the Canadian practices identified by Mr. Trump as problematic — the justification for his tariffs under the law — were, in fact, “not discrimination.”

The center also questioned whether the statute itself had essentially been rendered obsolete, pointing out the legal and legislative history that ultimately yielded Section 301.

To successfully invoke that section, the administration must first complete a full investigation that documents another country’s unfair practices. But, instead, by opting to use the more outdated Section 338, Mr. Trump essentially sought to speed up his ability to impose tariffs, according to the lawsuit, which accused the president of circumventing the will of Congress in the process.

“Congress did not intend to leave in place a parallel authority that would allow the president to impose the same remedies, for the same conduct, free of every one of those safeguards,” according to the lawsuit.

item.title: Heading to France? Amid Recent Unrest, Here’s What to Know.
item.description:
Anti-government demonstrations across France escalated into widespread violence over the weekend, as thousands of protesters clashed with police, set municipal buildings and cars on fire, and ransacked storefronts.

The unrest, which began last month as largely peaceful, student-led protests over the quality of the public education system, spiraled into the country’s worst rioting in decades, with more than 2,000 arrests and nearly 1,000 police officers injured, according to the French Interior Ministry. To reassert control, authorities issued curfews in parts of several cities on Monday, including Paris, Nice and Lille.

More demonstrations have been planned over the next two weeks. Here’s what you need to know if you plan to travel to France soon.

Paris became the epicenter of demonstrations over the weekend, with major clashes and rioting at Place de la République and surrounding avenues. Many of the shops across Les Halles were looted and vandalized, while the Place de la Bastille and Place de la Concorde became flash points for standoffs between the police and protesters.

Marseille, France’s second-largest city and a popular tourist destination, also saw significant unrest, with protesters breaking into City Hall and ransacking the building, leaving graffiti and knocking over the bust of Marianne, a symbol of the French Republic. In response, authorities banned public gatherings in the city between noon and 8 p.m.

In Lyon, tens of thousands of protesters marched through the city on Saturday, and some set fire to the city’s tourism office. Other major cities like Bordeaux, Lille, Calais and Limoges also experienced violence and damage to public buildings.

While Paris is generally considered safe, government travel advisories, including those from the State Department, urge citizens to avoid protest areas and exercise increased caution because of civil unrest. Travelers have also been advised to follow local media outlets for updates on planned demonstrations.

The next major protests are scheduled for Oct. 24, Oct. 31 and Nov. 5, with the Yellow Vests, a populist protest movement, calling for gatherings at Place de la Bastille and Place de la République, although times and routes have not been finalized and are awaiting police approval.

By Tuesday, major streets in central Paris had been cleaned up and Parisians had returned to work, although many storefront windows remained broken, and burned cars and bikes littered the streets. Parks, including Luxembourg Gardens, Tuileries Garden and Parc Monceau, were calm. At cafes, people sat on patios with coffee and wine, and tourists and tour guides went about their days as planned.

Sophie Gacheny, an independent tour guide based in the city, urged visitors to stay on the Left Bank, or the southern bank of the River Seine, which is typically quieter during protests. Like other guides, Ms. Gacheny is planning her tours around the protests and won’t run any on the days when demonstrations are scheduled.

Kiana Tiese, who offers private tours of Paris, said she took a group of visitors out for a tour on Sunday, a day after the protests, and said everything went well.

While most major Paris landmarks like the Eiffel Tower and Arc de Triomphe remain open, local authorities can close them on short notice if large-scale protests pass through them. On Monday, the Louvre was forced to shut down after protesters blocked the entrance, causing anger among tourists who had paid for their tickets. (The museum has not announced when it will reopen.)

The tourism board, Paris Je T’Aime, advises travelers to monitor live updates through its website and dedicated city pass app, which provide real-time updates on operating hours for major landmarks and venues.

Municipal buildings, shops and outdoor monuments have been damaged across other major cities, too, creating road closures and areas with restricted access. Be sure to check the status of a landmark and surrounding areas before traveling there.

French unions have called for a nationwide general strike on Nov. 5, which could affect the national rail, public transit networks and roads. Under French law, transportation workers must file notice of a strike at least 48 hours before the planned action.

On demonstration days, police shut down metro stations and roads along protest routes, and bus and tram schedules are reduced.

French authorities imposed curfews on Monday across parts of several major cities, including Paris, Lille, Lyon and Nice.

In Paris, the authorities enacted strict curfews in areas where demonstrations turned violent, such as Place de la République and the Les Halles commercial district. Authorities banned public gatherings in those areas between 8 p.m. and 6 a.m., and prohibited people from being in public outdoor spaces across dozens of districts between 11 p.m. Monday and 6 a.m. Tuesday. Police set up checkpoints around the perimeter of the curfew zones to verify the identities of residents and exempt emergency workers. It was unclear how long the curfews would last.

At the five-star Hotel Lancaster Paris, steps from the Champs-Élysées, hotel guests sipped drinks and ate French tapas on Monday night in the lobby’s plush Copperbay cocktail bar. The rest of the neighborhood was equally tranquil, with no police or sirens in sight. Along the tree-shaded grand boulevard, international crowds strolled under the wrought-iron streetlamps, window-shopping at big global stores like Sephora and Zara.

Lauren Bell, 38, who was visiting the city with her sister from Madrid over the weekend, said that while the city felt calm on Tuesday, people also seemed to be preparing for the next wave. “We were shocked to see how quickly and badly the situation got violent and out of control,” she said. “It feels like it’s not over.”

Whether your travel insurance will cover trip cancellation depends on your policy. Most standard policies don’t cover civil unrest, but if you purchased a “cancel for any reason” policy and meet the conditions, you may get reimbursed for your trip.

Ryley Ober and Seth Sherwood contributed reporting.

Follow New York Times Travel on Instagram and sign up for our Travel Dispatch newsletter to get expert tips on traveling smarter and inspiration for your next vacation. Dreaming up a future getaway or just armchair traveling? Check out our 52 Places to Go in 2026.
